cultivar: Local Yixing small-leaf population bushes, with introduced cultivars such as Fuding Dabai in newer gardens
processing: Fully oxidised small-leaf black: a bud with one or two spring leaves is withered, rolled, oxidised and dried gently, then lightly sorted.
harvest_season: Spring, from around Qingming to Guyu (April); a smaller autumn picking is made in some gardens.
appearance_dry: Small, tight, slightly curled dark strands with a scattering of golden tips.
appearance_wet: Small, tender copper-red leaves, even and soft.
taste_profile: Mild and honey-sweet with caramel and a light fruitiness, low tannin and a soft, clean finish; a gentle tea rather than a bold one.

brewing.notes: Locals brew it in a zisha pot, which suits its softness; 90 °C and short steeps. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 2.5–3 minutes, neat.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, mostly within Jiangsu and through zisha-teapot sellers; drink within a year. There is no grading ladder to speak of and no vintage market.
description:
Yixing is famous for its purple-clay teapots, and Yixing Hong Cha is the tea the potters drink from them. The town on the shore of Lake Tai in southern Jiangsu has grown tea since at least the Tang dynasty under the old name Yangxian, and today its hills are Jiangsu's main tea district; the black tea is a modern, modest product made for the domestic market, often sold under the broader name Su Hong, 'Jiangsu red'.

It is made from small-leaf local bushes – and increasingly from introduced cultivars such as Fuding Dabai – picked in spring as a bud with one or two leaves, then withered, rolled, oxidised and dried gently. The small leaf and gentle finish make it a soft tea: low in tannin, sweet, with none of the malt and muscle of a big-leaf black.

Expect honey and caramel, a light fruit note and a clean, mild finish over five or six short steeps; it is easy to drink and easy to over-steep into blandness rather than bitterness, so keep infusions short. It is often brewed in a small zisha pot, and because a clay pot rounds off edges a tea this soft loses little in one.

It is sold as the current spring, mostly in Jiangsu and from teapot sellers who throw a packet in with a pot, and it rarely travels abroad. There are no formal grades; buy by picking date and look for small, even, tippy leaf with a sweet dry aroma. A fair number of 'Yixing' blacks are made from leaf bought in from Zhejiang or Fujian, so a named garden is worth something.

If you have just bought a zisha pot, this is the tea the locals would season it with: forgiving, sweet and unlikely to leave a flavour you regret.
sources_note: A minor regional tea with thin documentation; cultivar mix and the Zhejiang/Fujian sourcing remark are generalised from Jiangsu vendor descriptions. Tang-era tea history refers to the Yangxian tribute tea, not to black tea.
